prompt: A loop attaches a click handler to each of several buttons using `for (var i = 0; i < buttons.length; i++) { buttons[i].addEventListener('click', () => alert(i)); }`. Every button alerts the same final number. Why?
choices: var is function/global scoped, so there is only one i shared by every callback, and by the time any button is clicked the loop has already finished and left i at its final value
addEventListener only remembers the last listener attached to any element, so earlier ones are discarded
let would produce the exact same bug, so switching to let would not fix it
Arrow functions cannot be used as event listener callbacks, which causes them all to fall back to the same handler

prompt: What does a JavaScript closure actually capture from its surrounding scope?
choices: A live reference to the variable binding itself, so later changes to that variable are visible inside the closure
A frozen copy of the variable's value at the exact moment the inner function was defined
Nothing — closures only work with global variables, never with local ones
A copy of the entire outer function's source code, re-parsed each time the closure runs
querySelectorAll returns a NodeList, which does not have map/filter/reduce; it needs to be converted with Array.from(...) first
map only works on arrays of numbers, never on arrays of DOM elements
querySelectorAll always returns null when more than one element matches the selector
The .item selector syntax is invalid, so querySelectorAll never returns any results

prompt: What is the key difference between document.querySelector and document.querySelectorAll?
choices: querySelector returns the first matching element (or null); querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of every matching element (possibly empty)
querySelector returns every match; querySelectorAll returns only the first match
querySelector only works on IDs; querySelectorAll only works on classes
They are interchangeable aliases for the exact same method

prompt: A `<ul>` of to-do items gets new `<li>` elements added dynamically after the page loads. Why attach a single click listener to the `<ul>` (event delegation) instead of one listener per `<li>`?
choices: Because a listener attached directly to an `<li>` that gets added later would never exist; one listener on the stable parent catches clicks on any child, present or future, via event.target
Because browsers silently ignore any listener attached to more than 10 elements at once
Because addEventListener can only be called once per page, no matter how many elements need listeners
Because click events do not bubble, so delegation is only cosmetic and changes nothing functionally

prompt: What problem do Promises solve compared to plain nested callbacks for handling something like a fetch() request?
choices: They let you chain .then()/.catch() instead of nesting callback after callback, with a single standardized way to handle success and failure
They make the network request finish instantly instead of taking time
They remove the need for addEventListener anywhere in the page
They convert asynchronous code into synchronous code that blocks the browser until it finishes

prompt: Given `const user = { name: 'Alex' }; user.name = 'Sam';` — does this throw an error?
choices: No — const prevents reassigning the variable user to a different object, but mutating properties of the object it already points to is still allowed
Yes — const freezes every property of any object assigned to it, so user.name can never change
Yes — const can only be used with primitive values like numbers and strings, never with objects
No, but only because 'name' is a special property name that const always allows changing
